title: How the GED Test Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the GED (General Educational Development) test: its origins in a World War II-era compromise between the American Council on Education and the military, its expansion to civilians, its revisions over decades (including the 2002 version and the 2014 overhaul), the shift to a for-profit model under Pearson, competing tests (TASC and HiSET), test format, cost and state subsidies, accommodations, and why people take it for jobs or college. The episode closes with listener mail about goats licking feet and a segment of off-topic banter about music and the A.V. Club's Undercover series.

segments.title: Opening banter on brand names and the GED name
segments.summary: The hosts joke about generic trademarks like Kleenex and Vaseline, then introduce the GED, noting it stands for General Educational Development rather than General Equivalency Diploma.

segments.title: Who takes the GED and why
segments.summary: The hosts cite statistics on test-takers and completers, the passing score set by comparing against high school seniors, the average delay of about nine years before taking it, and the reasons people take it for jobs, college, and personal satisfaction.

segments.title: Origins of the GED after World War II
segments.summary: The GED began as a compromise between the military and the American Council on Education, which opposed handing out wartime diplomas. It was initially for military service members before expanding to civilians.

segments.title: Revisions to the GED over the decades
segments.summary: The hosts describe how the test moved from basic skills to more real-world, conceptual content, added an essay component, separated reading tests, and was revised several times, with the most recent prior revision in 2002.

segments.title: College premium and the value of a degree
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how the number of GED takers seeking college versus employment has tracked the college wage premium and employer demand, and they debate whether college is worth the cost and student loan burden.

segments.title: Pearson takeover and GED privatization
segments.summary: The American Council on Education, which had run the GED as a nonprofit, handed it to for-profit publisher Pearson in 2014, ending the test's nonprofit status and creating competition with TASC and HiSET. Pearson raised fees, which the hosts say hit low-income test-takers hard.

segments.title: Computer-based testing and test format
segments.summary: The 2014 GED moved to a computer-based format with four subject modules covering reasoning through language arts, math, science, and social studies. Immediate scoring and retakes of individual modules are available, and the test takes about eight hours in total. Accommodations exist for disabilities and for test-takers who want a private room.

segments.title: Preparation, languages, and the 2014 math changes
segments.summary: The hosts discuss study materials, testing in other languages and formats such as Braille and large print, and the harder math section that now covers algebra two. A Florida test-taker waited to take the 2014 version for its challenge.

segments.title: Closing and listener mail
segments.summary: The hosts close with a call to action to look up the GED on the website, then read listener mail from Joachim in Denmark about goats licking the flesh off feet. Off-topic banter about music and the A.V. Club's Undercover series follows, along with sign-off remarks.
